items.name: pinneapple_systems.time_series.predictability.predictability_report
items.title: Forecast a noisy or near-random series without fooling yourself (predictability first, purged walk-forward, untouched test, DM tests)
items.summary: Predictability of a scalar series before any modelling.
items.description:
Predictability of a scalar series before any modelling.

The surrogate tests use the nonlinear prediction error at horizon 1 (one-sided: is the series more predictable
by nearest neighbours than its surrogates?) and the time-reversal asymmetry (two-sided). When the AR(1)
coefficient exceeds 0.99 and ``difference_if_unit_root`` is set, the tests and entropies run on the first
differences, because Fourier surrogates of a non-stationary series are not a valid null (Schreiber & Schmitz
2000, Physica D 142:346); ``tested_on`` says which.

items.name: pinneapple_neural.callbacks.PhysicsMonitor
items.title: Physics checks during training (Lightning, PhysicsNeMo, Hugging Face)
items.summary: The checks of ``pp.validate(model, problem, data, reference, query, level)`` as training metrics.
items.description:
The checks of ``pp.validate(model, problem, data, reference, query, level)`` as training metrics.

``every``: run the checks every this many steps. ``watch``: check ids whose value is tracked for the early warning
(default: every check with a numeric value; the direction that counts as better is the check's ``better`` in
``validation.schema``: lower |value| for errors, higher for coverages, spread ratios and crossing times).
``patience``: number of consecutive checks in which a watched metric worsened while the loss improved before the
warning fires (a step is checked once, also with gradient accumulation). ``action``: ``"warn"`` (a
:class:`PhysicsWarning`) or ``"stop"`` (also sets ``should_stop``). ``model_fn``: maps the framework's module to
the model to validate (e.g. ``lambda m: m.net`` for a LightningModule that wraps the network). ``report_path``:
where :meth:`finish` writes the report (JSON) and the trust card (``*.trust.json``).

Metrics are named ``physics/<check id>`` plus ``physics/n_fail`` and ``physics/n_warn``.

items.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.rollout.validate_rollout
items.title: Validate an autoregressive rollout (trust horizon, drift, long-run statistics)
items.summary: ``rollout.*`` checks of a model rollout (status pass / fail / not-applicable with evidence).
items.description:
``rollout.*`` checks of a model rollout (status pass / fail / not-applicable with evidence).

``ref``: the reference trajectory from the same initial state; ``conserved``: invariants that must stay constant
(checked without a reference; built-in names or keys of ``invariants``, a mapping ``name -> f(traj, ndim)``);
``ndim = 0``: the state is a vector (particles, a ROM's coefficients), with no spatial spectrum; ``long_ref``: a long reference run for the statistics of a chaotic system (the
model's run ``pred`` must be long too); ``chaotic``: after the pointwise error crosses its tolerance the two
trajectories are decorrelated, so a later spectral or invariant crossing compares two different states of the
attractor and is reported, not failed (``rollout.statistics`` judges that regime). Tolerances: ``error``, ``spectrum``, ``invariants`` (divergence time),
``drift`` (conserved invariants, relative), ``floor`` (statistics: allowed multiple of the noise floor).

items.title: 3-D cantilever with C3D8I hexahedra, against beam theory
items.summary: Numerical solvers, particle dynamics and bridges to OpenFOAM, CalculiX, FEniCS, MATLAB and FMUs.
items.description: `numerical_solvers` holds the in-house solvers: finite differences, finite volumes, lattice Boltzmann, spectral and FFT solvers, a 3-D finite-element solver with incompatible-mode hexahedra (`solid_fem`), internal pipe and mixer flow on OpenFOAM (`internal_flow`), DEM particles in a stirred tank (`particles`), and dataset generation for PINNs. `external_solvers` drives real tools when they are installed (OpenFOAM, CalculiX through `pp.fea`, FEniCS, MATLAB, Modelica/FMU) and degrades gracefully when they are not. `particle_dynamics` has differentiable rigid bodies, MPM and SPH in PyTorch. items.code:
import numpy as np
from pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.solid_fem import box_mesh, SolidFEM, fea_figure

L, W, H, F, E = 2.0, 0.1, 0.2, 1e4, 210e9
mesh = box_mesh(L, W, H, 40, 3, 6)
fem = SolidFEM(mesh, E=E, nu=0.3)
fem.fix(mesh.nodes_on(x=0.0))
fem.load_face(mesh.face_nodes("x+"), (0, 0, -F))
res = fem.solve()

I = W * H ** 3 / 12
G = E / 2.6
theory = F * L ** 3 / (3 * E * I) + F * L / (5 / 6 * G * W * H)    # Euler-Bernoulli + shear (Timoshenko)
print(f"tip deflection {res.max_displacement * 1e3:.3f} mm, Timoshenko {theory * 1e3:.3f} mm")
print(f"max von Mises {res.von_mises.max() / 1e6:.1f} MPa, beam theory at the root {F * L * H / 2 / I / 1e6:.1f} MPa")
fig = fea_figure(res, "von_mises")

items.name: pinneapple_lab__0
items.title: A minimal experiment with a reference check
items.summary: Run experiments reproducibly, check them, and grow a database of results, datasets and trust cards.
items.description: An experiment is a class with parameters and a `run(ctx)` method. The runner gives every run an id from the experiment, its version and its parameters, and records inputs, outputs, metrics, checks, figures and datasets in one folder indexed in SQLite. Checks have a kind (physics, reference, baseline, sanity, generalisation, uncertainty), and curation turns them into a tier (A to D) and a six-stage trust card: data and geometry, model, physical constraints, benchmark, uncertainty and engineering decision. `uq` adds coverage of predictive intervals and grid convergence indices. `python -m pinneapple_lab site` writes the public catalogue.
items.code:
import json, math, os, tempfile
from pinneapple_lab import Experiment, register, run

@register
class Pendulum(Experiment):
    name = "pendulum_doc_example"
    params = {"L": 1.0, "theta0": 0.05}
    def run(self, ctx):
        L, th = ctx.params["L"], ctx.params["theta0"]
        T = 2 * math.pi * math.sqrt(L / 9.81) * (1 + th ** 2 / 16)       # small-angle period + first correction
        ctx.metric("period_s", T)
        ctx.check("period_matches_small_angle", value=T / (2 * math.pi * math.sqrt(L / 9.81)),
                  min=0.999, max=1.002, kind="reference", detail="T vs 2 pi sqrt(L/g)")

root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
r = run("pendulum_doc_example", {"L": 2.0}, root=root)
print(r.status, {k: round(v, 4) for k, v in r.metrics.items()})
checks = json.load(open(os.path.join(r.dir, "validation.json")))
print([(c["name"], c["passed"], c["kind"]) for c in checks])
print("run folder:", sorted(os.listdir(r.dir)))

items.name: pinneapple_physics__0
items.title: Burgers' equation: a PINN against the Cole-Hopf solution, through one API
items.summary: Define a physical problem once, solve it with a PINN, a solver or a closed form, and compare.
items.description: `pde_environment` describes a problem as a `ProblemSpec`: the PDE terms, the boundary and initial conditions, data constraints and scales, with presets for Navier-Stokes, heat, wave, Burgers, elasticity, Helmholtz and RANS turbulence models. `pinn_solver` compiles a spec into differentiable losses, and `symbolic_pde` turns SymPy expressions into autograd residuals. Not every engineering question needs a PDE. `closed_form` holds textbook models (fins, beams and fatigue, Helmholtz resonators, heat sinks, PCB thermal) as fast ground truth, and `tribology` solves sliding wear with contact-pressure redistribution. Domain packages (`weather`, `blackhole`, `pcb`) build on the same pieces.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pinneapple as pp

pinn = pp.solve("burgers_1d", method="pinn", epochs=3000)
exact = pp.solve("burgers_1d", method="analytic")
def trained_pinn(problem, **kw):            # compare() takes method names or callables returning a Solution
    return pinn
print(pp.compare("burgers_1d", methods=[trained_pinn], reference=exact))

x = np.linspace(-1, 1, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3))
for t in (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75):
    X = np.column_stack([x, np.full_like(x, t)])
    l, = ax.plot(x, exact.predict(X)[:, 0], lw=2.2, alpha=0.5)
    ax.plot(x, pinn.predict(X)[:, 0], "--", c=l.get_color(), label=f"t = {t}")
ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("u"); ax.legend(fontsize=7); ax.set_title("PINN (dashed) vs Cole-Hopf (solid)")

items.title: Conformal prediction: intervals with guaranteed coverage around any model
items.summary: Uncertainty, validation, inverse problems, equation discovery, state estimation and trust scores.
items.description: `uncertainty` covers aleatoric heads, MC dropout, deep ensembles, conformal prediction, quantile regression and calibration metrics, behind one `uq_predict` entry point. `validation` checks physical consistency: conservation, boundary conditions, symmetry and agreement with analytical or solver references. `inverse_problems` estimates parameters from observations (noise models, Tikhonov / TV regularisation with L-curve, local and Sobol sensitivity, ensemble Kalman inversion) and discovers missing terms with SINDy. `state_estimation` has extended and ensemble Kalman filters. `trust` scores a model's predictions before anyone consumes them.

items.name: pinneapple_neural__2

items.summary: Architectures, training and inference: PINNs, neural operators, GNNs and reduced-order models.
items.description: `architectures` has the model families behind one registry (`ModelRegistry.build(name, ...)`): PINN networks (MLP, SIREN, modified MLP, Fourier features, hash grids, PINNsFormer), neural operators (FNO, AFNO, DeepONet and multi-scale DeepONet), graph networks (MeshGraphNet, equivariant GNNs) and reduced-order models (POD, DMD, Operator Inference, SINDy, HAVOK, Koopman, parametric POD-RBF/GPR). `trainer` gives the training loops (two-phase Adam then L-BFGS, time marching, causal weighting, DDP and FSDP), loss balancing (GradNorm, NTK, self-adaptive weights) and callbacks. `predictor` evaluates trained models on grids and draws the results.

items.name: pinneapple_security__0
items.title: Digest, sign and verify a result; redact personal data from a log
items.summary: Integrity, signatures, provenance, audit trails, encryption and privacy for scientific data.
items.description: SHA-256 digests and Merkle manifests of files, arrays and model folders; Ed25519 or HMAC signatures in DSSE envelopes; in-toto / SLSA provenance of runs and a CycloneDX SBOM; a hash-chained audit trail; AES-256-GCM at rest; PII detection (including CPF and CNPJ), redaction and k-anonymity; differential privacy; safe loading of checkpoints and secret scanning.
items.code:
import numpy as np
from pinneapple_security import digest_array, hmac_key, sign_json, verify_json, redact

field = np.linspace(0, 1, 1000)
d = digest_array(field)
key = hmac_key(b"a-shared-secret-of-32-bytes-.....")
env = sign_json({"result": "Kt = 2.59", "field_sha256": d}, key)
print("payload verified:", verify_json(env, key))
env["payload"] = env["payload"][:-4] + "AAAA"
try:
    verify_json(env, key)
except Exception as e:
    print("tampered envelope rejected:", type(e).__name__)
print(redact("run by maria.silva@example.com, CPF 123.456.789-09, phone +55 11 91234-5678"))

items.name: pinneapple_quantum__0
items.title: Exact harmonic-oscillator states used as the reference
items.summary: Variational quantum circuits as physics-informed models: VQ-PINN, hybrid PINN, Hamiltonian learning.
items.description: A variational circuit is the ansatz of a wavefunction and the loss is the Rayleigh quotient (the VQE objective) or a PDE residual, on simulators or real hardware through pluggable back-ends. Presets cover the Schrodinger equation in 1-D and 2-D (ground and excited states), hybrid classical-quantum networks, Hamiltonian learning from energy data and quantum-kernel PINNs. Exact solutions (harmonic oscillator, spin chains) ship with the package so every quantum result has a reference.
items.code:
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pinneapple_quantum import exact_eigenstates_1d_harmonic

x = torch.linspace(-5, 5, 400)[:, None]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
for n in range(4):
    psi, E = exact_eigenstates_1d_harmonic(x, n_state=n)

    ax.plot(x, 0.6 * psi.squeeze() + E, label=f"n = {n}"); ax.axhline(E, c="0.8", lw=0.6)
ax.plot(x, 0.5 * x ** 2, "k", lw=0.8); ax.set_ylim(0, 4.5); ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("E, psi (offset)")

items.name: pinneapple_analysis__2
items.title: Extended Kalman filter tracking a pendulum from noisy angle readings
items.summary: Uncertainty, validation, inverse problems, equation discovery, state estimation and trust scores.
items.description: `uncertainty` covers aleatoric heads, MC dropout, deep ensembles, conformal prediction, quantile regression and calibration metrics, behind one `uq_predict` entry point. `validation` checks physical consistency: conservation, boundary conditions, symmetry and agreement with analytical or solver references. `inverse_problems` estimates parameters from observations (noise models, Tikhonov / TV regularisation with L-curve, local and Sobol sensitivity, ensemble Kalman inversion) and discovers missing terms with SINDy. `state_estimation` has extended and ensemble Kalman filters. `trust` scores a model's predictions before anyone consumes them.
items.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.kalman import ExtendedKalmanFilter

dt, g_L = 0.02, 9.81
f = lambda s: np.array([s[0] + dt * s[1], s[1] - dt * g_L * np.sin(s[0])])
h = lambda s: s[:1]
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
truth = [np.array([1.0, 0.0])]
for _ in range(400):
    truth.append(f(truth[-1]))
truth = np.array(truth)
obs = truth[:, :1] + rng.normal(0, 0.15, (len(truth), 1))

ekf = ExtendedKalmanFilter(2, 1, f, h, Q=np.eye(2) * 1e-5, R=np.eye(1) * 0.15 ** 2)
ekf.initialize(np.array([0.5, 0.0]), np.eye(2))
est = []
for y in obs:
    ekf.step(y); est.append(ekf.x.copy())
est = np.array(est)
print(f"angle RMS error: raw readings {np.sqrt(np.mean((obs[:, 0] - truth[:, 0]) ** 2)):.3f} rad,"
      f" filter {np.sqrt(np.mean((est[100:, 0] - truth[100:, 0]) ** 2)):.3f} rad (after spin-up)")
print(f"angular velocity is never measured; filter RMS error {np.sqrt(np.mean((est[100:, 1] - truth[100:, 1]) ** 2)):.3f} rad/s")

tt = np.arange(len(truth)) * dt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8))
ax.plot(tt, obs[:, 0], ".", ms=2, c="0.6", label="readings"); ax.plot(tt, truth[:, 0], label="truth")
ax.plot(tt, est[:, 0], "--", label="EKF"); ax.set_xlabel("t (s)"); ax.set_ylabel("angle (rad)"); ax.legend(ncol=3, fontsize=7)

reference_run.stdout:

angular velocity is never measured; filter RMS error 0.048 rad/s

items.name: pinneapple_core__0
items.title: Gradient and integral of a field on a grid, checked against calculus
items.summary: Domain, Geometry, Mesh and Field: one vocabulary for tensors, geometry and topology.
items.description: Physics AI keeps passing the same things around: a region, points sampled in it, values on a grid, a mesh or a point cloud, and derivatives of those values. `pinneapple_core` gives them one interface. A `Field` answers `gradient()`, `divergence()`, `interpolate(x)` and `integrate()` whatever it is stored on (regular grid, simplex mesh with exact P1 operators, or scattered points with local least squares). `FunctionField` gives the same interface to a torch callable such as a PINN, through autograd. The free functions in `operators` (`grad`, `div`, `curl`, `laplacian`, `integrate`, `flux`) work on all of them.
items.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pinneapple_core import Field, Domain

x = np.linspace(0, 1, 101); y = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y, indexing="ij")
u = np.sin(np.pi * X) * np.sin(np.pi * Y)
f = Field.on_grid([x, y], u, name="u")

g = f.gradient().values.reshape(101, 101, 2)   # (points, component, dim) -> grid
exact = np.pi * np.cos(np.pi * X) * np.sin(np.pi * Y)
print("max |du/dx - exact| =", float(np.abs(g[..., 0] - exact).max()))
print("integral =", float(f.integrate()), " exact 4/pi^2 =", 4 / np.pi ** 2)

d = Domain.box([0, 0], [1, 1])
pts = d.sample_interior(5, seed=0)
print("u at random points:", np.round(f.interpolate(pts), 4))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.4))
for a, val, t in [(ax[0], u, "u = sin(pi x) sin(pi y)"), (ax[1], np.hypot(g[..., 0], g[..., 1]), "|grad u|")]:
    im = a.pcolormesh(X, Y, val, shading="auto", cmap="viridis"); a.set_title(t); a.set_aspect("equal")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=a, shrink=0.85)

items.name: pinneapple_lab__1
items.title: Grid convergence index of a mesh study (Celik et al. 2008)
items.summary: Run experiments reproducibly, check them, and grow a database of results, datasets and trust cards.
items.description: An experiment is a class with parameters and a `run(ctx)` method. The runner gives every run an id from the experiment, its version and its parameters, and records inputs, outputs, metrics, checks, figures and datasets in one folder indexed in SQLite. Checks have a kind (physics, reference, baseline, sanity, generalisation, uncertainty), and curation turns them into a tier (A to D) and a six-stage trust card: data and geometry, model, physical constraints, benchmark, uncertainty and engineering decision. `uq` adds coverage of predictive intervals and grid convergence indices. `python -m pinneapple_lab site` writes the public catalogue.

from pinneapple_lab.uq import gci, coverage

g = gci([2.512, 2.571, 2.591], h=[4.0, 2.0, 1.0])          # coarse -> fine

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
y = rng.normal(size=2000); mean = np.zeros(2000)
print("coverage of a calibrated 90 % interval:", round(coverage(y, mean, np.ones(2000), 0.9), 3))
print("coverage of an over-confident one:     ", round(coverage(y, mean, 0.5 * np.ones(2000), 0.9), 3))

items.name: pinneapple_neural__1
items.title: Parametric POD with Gaussian-process uncertainty, against the nearest-design baseline
items.summary: Architectures, training and inference: PINNs, neural operators, GNNs and reduced-order models.
items.description: `architectures` has the model families behind one registry (`ModelRegistry.build(name, ...)`): PINN networks (MLP, SIREN, modified MLP, Fourier features, hash grids, PINNsFormer), neural operators (FNO, AFNO, DeepONet and multi-scale DeepONet), graph networks (MeshGraphNet, equivariant GNNs) and reduced-order models (POD, DMD, Operator Inference, SINDy, HAVOK, Koopman, parametric POD-RBF/GPR). `trainer` gives the training loops (two-phase Adam then L-BFGS, time marching, causal weighting, DDP and FSDP), loss balancing (GradNorm, NTK, self-adaptive weights) and callbacks. `predictor` evaluates trained models on grids and draws the results.
items.code:
import numpy as np
from pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom import ParametricPOD, latin_hypercube

x = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
def field(p):                                         # deflection-like response of two design parameters
    a, b = p
    return a * np.sin(np.pi * x) + b * x ** 2 * (1 - x)

P, names = latin_hypercube(40, {"a": (0.5, 2.0), "b": (-1.0, 1.0)}, seed=0)
Xs = np.array([field(p) for p in P])
Pt, _ = latin_hypercube(20, {"a": (0.5, 2.0), "b": (-1.0, 1.0)}, seed=1)
Xt = np.array([field(p) for p in Pt])

gpr = ParametricPOD(regressor="gpr").fit(P, Xs)
near = ParametricPOD(regressor="nearest").fit(P, Xs)
print("modes kept:", gpr.rank, " energy:", round(gpr.energy_captured, 8))
print(f"median error  POD-GPR {np.median(gpr.error(Pt, Xt)):.2e}   nearest design {np.median(near.error(Pt, Xt)):.2e}")
_, std = gpr.predict(Pt[:1], return_std=True)
print("predictive std available:", std.shape)

reference_run.stdout:
modes kept: 2  energy: 1.0
median error  POD-GPR 4.77e-07   nearest design 7.08e-02

items.name: pinneapple_neural__0
items.title: POD + DMD of a travelling wave: compress, then forecast
items.summary: Architectures, training and inference: PINNs, neural operators, GNNs and reduced-order models.
items.description: `architectures` has the model families behind one registry (`ModelRegistry.build(name, ...)`): PINN networks (MLP, SIREN, modified MLP, Fourier features, hash grids, PINNsFormer), neural operators (FNO, AFNO, DeepONet and multi-scale DeepONet), graph networks (MeshGraphNet, equivariant GNNs) and reduced-order models (POD, DMD, Operator Inference, SINDy, HAVOK, Koopman, parametric POD-RBF/GPR). `trainer` gives the training loops (two-phase Adam then L-BFGS, time marching, causal weighting, DDP and FSDP), loss balancing (GradNorm, NTK, self-adaptive weights) and callbacks. `predictor` evaluates trained models on grids and draws the results.
items.code:
import numpy as np, torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom import POD, DynamicModeDecomposition

x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 256); t = np.arange(0, 12, 0.05)
U = np.array([np.sin(x - 1.3 * s) + 0.5 * np.sin(3 * x + 2.1 * s) for s in t])   # (T, D)
X = torch.tensor(U, dtype=torch.float64)

pod = POD(r=8).fit(X[:160])
print("POD energy in 4 modes:", float(pod.explained_variance_ratio_[:4].sum()))

dmd = DynamicModeDecomposition(r=4, center=False).fit(X[:160])
pred = dmd.rollout(X[159:160], steps=len(t) - 160)[0, 1:]
err = torch.linalg.norm(pred - X[160:]) / torch.linalg.norm(X[160:])
print(f"DMD forecast error over {len(t) - 160} unseen steps: {float(err):.2e}")
print("DMD frequencies (Hz):", np.round(np.sort(np.abs(dmd.frequencies(dt=0.05).numpy())), 4))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.5, 3.2), sharey=True)
ax[0].imshow(U[160:], aspect="auto", cmap="RdBu_r", extent=[0, 2 * np.pi, t[-1], t[160]]); ax[0].set_title("truth")
ax[1].imshow(pred.numpy(), aspect="auto", cmap="RdBu_r", extent=[0, 2 * np.pi, t[-1], t[160]]); ax[1].set_title("DMD forecast")
ax[0].set_ylabel("t (unseen)"); [a.set_xlabel("x") for a in ax]

items.name: pinneapple_analysis__1
items.title: SINDy: recover the missing term of a damped oscillator from data
items.summary: Uncertainty, validation, inverse problems, equation discovery, state estimation and trust scores.
items.description: `uncertainty` covers aleatoric heads, MC dropout, deep ensembles, conformal prediction, quantile regression and calibration metrics, behind one `uq_predict` entry point. `validation` checks physical consistency: conservation, boundary conditions, symmetry and agreement with analytical or solver references. `inverse_problems` estimates parameters from observations (noise models, Tikhonov / TV regularisation with L-curve, local and Sobol sensitivity, ensemble Kalman inversion) and discovers missing terms with SINDy. `state_estimation` has extended and ensemble Kalman filters. `trust` scores a model's predictions before anyone consumes them.
items.code:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pinneapple_analysis import CandidateLibrary, SINDyIdentifier

t = np.linspace(0, 20, 2000)
x = np.exp(-0.1 * t) * np.cos(2 * t)
v = np.gradient(x, t, edge_order=2); a = np.gradient(v, t, edge_order=2)
t, x, v, a = (z[5:-5] for z in (t, x, v, a))        # finite differences are least accurate at the ends
# known part of the model: a = -4 x ; the residual holds what the model misses
b = a + 4 * x
Theta, names = CandidateLibrary(poly_order=2).build(np.column_stack([x, v]))
names = [n.replace("x0", "x").replace("x1", "v") for n in names]
res = SINDyIdentifier(threshold=0.05).fit(Theta, b, names)
print(res.equation("a + 4x"))
print("true:  a + 4x = -0.2 v - 0.01 x   (x = exp(-0.1 t) cos 2t solves x'' + 0.2 x' + 4.01 x = 0)")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 2.8))
ax.plot(t, b, lw=2, label="residual from data"); ax.plot(t, Theta @ res.coefficients, "--", label="SINDy model")
ax.set_xlabel("t"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("discovered damping term")

items.code:
import numpy as np
import pinneapple as pp
from pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.builder import ProblemBuilder

# laplace(u) = f on the unit square, u = 0 on the boundary, exact u = sin(pi x) sin(pi y)
spec = (ProblemBuilder("poisson").domain(x=(0, 1), y=(0, 1)).fields("u").pde("poisson")
        .bc("dirichlet", field="u", value=0.0, on="x_boundary")
        .bc("dirichlet", field="u", value=0.0, on="y_boundary").build())
problem = pp.PhysicalProblem.from_pde_spec(spec)
ctx = {"source_fn": lambda X, ctx=None: -2 * np.pi**2 * np.sin(np.pi * X[:, 0]) * np.sin(np.pi * X[:, 1])}
exact = lambda X: (np.sin(np.pi * X[:, 0]) * np.sin(np.pi * X[:, 1]))[:, None]

fem = pp.solve(problem, "fem", ctx=ctx, n=24)
pinn = pp.solve(problem, "pinn", ctx=ctx, epochs=200, hidden_dim=16, n_layers=2, n_collocation=256)
table = pp.compare(problem, [fem, pinn], reference="exact", options={"exact": {"fn": exact}})
print(table)                                   # relative L2, RMSE, max error, train and inference cost
assert table.best() == "fem"

items.name: pinneapple_llm__0
items.title: The guardrail accepts a harmonic function and rejects one that is not
items.summary: Language models draft problems, geometry and twins from PINNeAPPle's own presets; a physics guardrail checks every result.
items.description: The language model only selects and parametrises what the library already implements (problem presets, geometry generators, twin configurations); it never invents physics. `research` searches the literature, `agent_loop` runs a tool-using loop, and `local_llm` with `conversation_store` keeps everything on your machine (Ollama and SQLite), with `finetune` for LoRA on the logged data. `PhysicsGuardrail` is the part that matters with or without an LLM: it re-evaluates the PDE residual on fresh points, checks units and conservation where a closed form exists, compares with reference data, and refuses to call a result trustworthy unless every applicable check passes, naming the one that failed.
items.code:
import torch
from pinneapple_llm import PhysicsGuardrail
from pinneapple_physics import get_preset

spec = get_preset("laplace_2d")                            # laplace(u) = 0 on the unit square
good = lambda X: (X[:, :1] ** 2 - X[:, 1:2] ** 2)           # x^2 - y^2 is harmonic
bad = lambda X: (X[:, :1] ** 2 + X[:, 1:2] ** 2)            # laplacian = 4
class Formula(torch.nn.Module):                            # any torch module works; this one has no weights
    def __init__(self, f):
        super().__init__(); self.f = f
    def forward(self, X):
        return self.f(X)

for name, f in [("x^2 - y^2", good), ("x^2 + y^2", bad)]:
    model = Formula(f)
    rep = PhysicsGuardrail(spec, residual_threshold=1e-3).check(model)
    pde = [c for c in rep.checks if "residual" in c.name][0]
    print(f"{name}: residual check passed={pde.passed}  ({pde.name}, value {pde.value:.3g})")

T = np.sin(np.pi * X) * np.sinh(np.pi * Y) / np.sinh(np.pi)          # any field on a grid, from any code

card = pp.trust_card({"x": x, "y": y}, T, pde="laplace",
                     dirichlet={"x_min": 0.0, "x_max": 0.0, "y_min": 0.0,
                                "y_max": lambda P: np.sin(np.pi * P[:, 0])},
                     train_bounds={"x": (0, 1), "y": (0, 1)})
print(card)                                    # one line per check, PASS / FAIL / N/A
assert card.decision == "APPROVED"

bad = pp.trust_card({"x": x, "y": y}, 1.2 * T, pde="laplace", dirichlet={"y_max": lambda P: np.sin(np.pi * P[:, 0])})
assert bad.decision == "REJECT"                # harmonic, but the boundary condition is wrong

items.name: pinneapple_decision__0
items.title: Which model for a parametric airfoil study?
items.summary: Choose the next experiment from a closed set of options, under hard constraints and verification.
items.description: The decision layer never predicts a physical result. It decides which experiment to run next (model, training strategy, validation): every option passes hard constraints first (a structured-grid FNO is excluded on an unstructured mesh), every executed result goes through a verifier, and only verified results become evidence for the next decision. Decisions are distributions over the options with the rationale and the facts that were not known, so a default is never mistaken for a fact about the problem.
items.code:
from pinneapple_decision import decide

d = decide({"description": "2D airfoil, surrogate over angle of attack", "reynolds": 1e5,
            "representation": "unstructured_mesh", "n_simulations": 200,
            "needs_parameter_generalization": True}, objective="choose physics model")
print("selected:", d.selected)
print("probabilities:", {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in d.probabilities.items()})
for k, why in list(d.excluded.items())[:2]:
    print("excluded", k, "->", why[:90])
print("requires validation:", d.requires_validation)

items.code:
from pinneapple_reason import cases, reason

chain = reason(*cases.roof())                  # flat tiles -> pitch -> ventilated ceiling -> radiant barrier
print(chain.explain("en"))                     # every step: the failure, its mechanism and numbers, the fix, why

run.stdout:
Roof: from flat tiles to a working roof

Requirements:
  R1: keep the design rain out of the room [lap_water_ingress]
  R2: no condensation dripping into the room [underside_condensation]
  R3: no radiant discomfort from the ceiling on a sunny day [radiant_heat_gain]

Version 0 (tiles):
  rain ingress through the lap fails: Water climbs the 1 mm gap of the lap by capillarity up to 14 mm, the wind pushes it 6.15 mm further and with no slope nothing drives the water off: the design storm ponds 25 mm: the total head (14 + 6.15 + 25 = 45.1 mm) exceeds the 0 mm the 75 mm lap rises at 0°. Water gets over the lap and drips inside.
  [proof: capillary + wind + film head 45.1 mm > height the lap rises 0 mm; hydraulic barrier of a lapped joint: capillary rise between plates + wind head + Nusselt film / ponding vs lap rise]
  Options tried:
    - increase_slope: fixes (margin -1 -> 0.358), cost: +7.9 % roof area (index 0.079)
    - longer_lap: infeasible (with no slope no lap lifts the water (L sin 0 = 0))
  So: pitch the roof to the material's minimum slope — gravity now drains the water (thin film instead of a pond) and the lap gains height (L sin(alpha)) against capillarity and wind
  -> slope_deg = 22.0
  (chosen: fixes the failure without breaking any requirement that passed)

Version 1 (tiles, pitch):
  condensation under the roof fails: On a clear night the tile radiates to the sky at -1.74 °C and cools to 14.2 °C; the tile underside, in contact with the room air, sits at 14.9 °C, below the dew point of the room air (16.4 °C at 21 °C and 75 %): vapour condenses and drips into the room.
  [proof: dew point of the room air 16.4 °C > temperature of the surface facing the room 14.9 °C; steady roof heat-balance network (clear night) + Magnus dew point]
  Options tried:
    - ceiling_ventilated_attic: fixes (margin -0.316 -> 0.37), cost: 1 m^2 of ceiling per m^2 of plan (index 1.5)
    - ceiling_insulation: infeasible (needs first: ceiling)
  So: ceiling with a ventilated attic — room air no longer touches the cold (or hot) tile: a ventilated attic and the ceiling sit in between, and the ceiling, fed by the tile's radiation, faces the room much closer to the air temperature
  (chosen: fixes the failure without breaking any requirement that passed)

Version 2 (tiles, pitch, ceiling):
  radiant heat gain from the roof fails: The 900 W/m^2 sun heats the tile to 59.1 °C; the ceiling above the occupants sits at 39 °C, 12 K above the room air (27 °C), more than the 5 K of radiant asymmetry acceptable for a warm ceiling: it pours 78.7 W/m^2 into the room.
  [proof: ceiling radiant asymmetry 12.0 K > comfort limit (warm ceiling) 5 K; steady roof heat-balance network (clear day, sun on the roof)]
  Options tried:
    - ceiling_ventilated_attic: infeasible (the concept already has 'ceiling')
    - radiant_barrier: fixes (margin -1.402 -> 0.482), cost: 1 m^2 of foil per m^2 of roof (index 0.4)
    - ceiling_insulation: fixes (margin -1.402 -> 0.438), cost: 50 mm of mineral wool on the ceiling (index 0.4)
  So: radiant barrier (low-emissivity foil under the tiles) — the tile underside gets an emissivity of ~0.05: tile-to-ceiling radiation, the dominant path, drops by an order of magnitude
  -> tile_under_emissivity = 0.05
  (chosen: fixes the failure without breaking any requirement that passed; of 2 options that fix it, it is the cheapest (0.4, 3 checks passing; vs ceiling_insulation: 3 passing, cost 0.4))

Version 3 (tiles, pitch, ceiling, radiant barrier):
  Every requirement passes.
  - R1/lap_water_ingress: 20.7 <= 28.1 mm
  - R2/underside_condensation: 16.4 <= 19.2 °C
  - R3/radiant_heat_gain: 2.591 <= 5 K

items.title: Write a coloured point cloud with a scalar property
items.summary: Export fields and trajectories as PLY sequences and build Blender scenes from them.
items.description: `export` writes point clouds and trajectories as PLY files with colours and extra scalar properties, in pure Python. `render` drives a local Blender installation through a subprocess to build and save a scene, the same pattern the studio uses for Cycles renders.
items.code:
import os, tempfile
import numpy as np
from pinneapple_blender import write_ply

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pts = rng.normal(size=(1000, 3)).astype(np.float32)
speed = np.linalg.norm(pts, axis=1)
col = (255 * np.column_stack([speed / speed.max(), 0.3 * np.ones(1000), 1 - speed / speed.max()])).astype(np.uint8)
path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "cloud.ply")
write_ply(path, pts, colors=col, scalar_fields={"speed": speed})
print(open(path, "rb").read(260).split(b"end_header")[0].decode())

items.name: burgers_1d_li2021
items.title: 1-D viscous Burgers, Li et al. (2021) operator-learning benchmark (1200 trajectories, 1024 points)
items.summary: u_t + (u^2/2)_x = nu u_xx on the periodic interval [0, 1), nu = 0.1, t in [0, 1]. Initial conditions u0 ~ N(0, 625 (-Laplacian + 25 I)^-2), the input distribution stated in Li et…
items.description: u_t + (u^2/2)_x = nu u_xx on the periodic interval [0, 1), nu = 0.1, t in [0, 1]. Initial conditions u0 ~ N(0, 625 (-Laplacian + 25 I)^-2), the input distribution stated in Li et al. (2021), section 5.1 (their released generator used alpha 2.5, tau 7, sigma 49 instead; this dataset follows the paper's text). The standard task maps u0 to u(., 1); the 11 snapshots t = 0, 0.1, ..., 1 are stored for time-dependent models. Grid x_j = j / 1024, j = 0..1023; u[:, 0] equals u0.

quality.label: source verified
quality.verification: Solver (Fourier pseudo-spectral, 2/3 dealiasing, ETDRK4) checked in tests/test_operator_benchmarks.py against the Cole-Hopf exact solution (max error < 1e-8) and for exact mean conservation. Resolution and time-step study on 4 held-aside inputs against a reference with 4096 points and dt 2.5e-5, all 10 saved times: the dataset setting (1024 points, dt 1e-4) has max rel. L2 error 4.4e-12; halving dt gives 6.3e-13, doubling the points 4.4e-12 (time-step limited, spectrally converged in space). Mean conserved to 8e-17. Stored in float32 (rounding ~6e-8 relative), far below the 1e-3 to 1e-2 errors operator-learning methods reach on this task (scripts/zoo/operator_data.py convergence).

items.name: darcy_2d_li2021
items.title: 2-D Darcy flow, Li et al. (2021) operator-learning benchmark (1200 coefficient / pressure pairs, 128 x 128)
items.summary: -div(a grad u) = 1 on the unit square, u = 0 on the boundary. Coefficients a = 12 where g >= 0 and 3 where g < 0, g ~ N(0, (-Laplacian + 9 I)^-2) (Li et al. 2021, section 5.2). g…
items.description: -div(a grad u) = 1 on the unit square, u = 0 on the boundary. Coefficients a = 12 where g >= 0 and 3 where g < 0, g ~ N(0, (-Laplacian + 9 I)^-2) (Li et al. 2021, section 5.2). g is drawn as a periodic Gaussian random field on the 128 x 128 cell grid (Li et al. use a cosine expansion on 421 nodes), so a is piecewise constant on the cells of the stored grid. The task maps a to u. Cell centres ((i + 1/2) / 128, (j + 1/2) / 128); u is the cell average of the solution.

quality.label: source verified
quality.verification: Solver (cell-centred two-point-flux finite volumes, harmonic face coefficients, sparse direct solve) checked in tests/test_operator_benchmarks.py on a manufactured variable-coefficient solution (second order, max error < 2e-3 at 64^2). Each sample is solved on the 512^2 grid (the piecewise-constant coefficient is represented exactly on every refinement) and averaged onto its 128^2 cells. Grid study on 4 held-aside inputs against 1024^2: max rel. L2 error 4.6e-3 (128^2), 1.6e-3 (256^2), 4.3e-4 (512^2, the dataset); observed order 1.36 / 1.21 (reduced from 2 by the coefficient jumps); Richardson estimate of the dataset's discretisation error ~8e-4 rel. L2, ten times below the ~1e-2 operator-learning methods reach on this task. u > 0 and below the a = 3 bound 1/24 in every sample.

items.name: navier_stokes_2d_li2021_nu1e-3
items.title: 2-D incompressible Navier-Stokes (vorticity), nu = 1e-3, Li et al. (2021) benchmark (1200 runs, 64 x 64, t 0-50)
items.summary: w_t + u . grad w = nu Laplacian(w) + f on the periodic unit square, u = (psi_y, -psi_x), -Laplacian(psi) = w, nu = 1e-3, f(x, y) = 0.1 (sin 2 pi (x + y) + cos 2 pi (x + y)), w0 ~…
items.description: w_t + u . grad w = nu Laplacian(w) + f on the periodic unit square, u = (psi_y, -psi_x), -Laplacian(psi) = w, nu = 1e-3, f(x, y) = 0.1 (sin 2 pi (x + y) + cos 2 pi (x + y)), w0 ~ N(0, 7^(3/2) (-Laplacian + 49 I)^-2.5) (Li et al. 2021, section 5.3). Solved on 128 x 128 and stored on the 64 x 64 grid x_i = i / 64 at t = 0, 1, ..., 50 (51 snapshots; w[:, 0] is w0). The usual task maps the first 10 snapshots to the next 40, or w0 to w(., 50).

quality.label: source verified
quality.verification: Solver (Fourier pseudo-spectral, 2/3 dealiasing, ETDRK4) checked in tests/test_operator_benchmarks.py: exact decay of a Taylor-Green vortex (1e-10) and a mean-free, finite forced flow. Resolution and time-step study on 4 held-aside inputs against a 256^2, dt 5e-3 reference at the stored 64^2 nodes and all 50 saved times: the dataset setting (128^2, dt 5e-2) has max rel. L2 error 4.0e-8 (6.6e-8 at t = 50); dt 2.5e-2 gives 2.5e-9 and dt 1e-2 6.0e-11 (fourth-order time convergence, the error is the time step's; the 128^2 grid is spectrally converged); solving directly on 64^2 would give 1.7e-4. Inputs are band-limited (Nyquist modes removed), so the 128^2 and 256^2 runs start from the same field. Every stored field is finite with spatial mean below 5e-8. Stored in float32 (~6e-8 relative), far below the 8e-3 or more operator-learning methods reach on this task.

items.title: Accretion onto a Schwarzschild black hole: 2.5-D viscous hydro density frames (256 x 128)
items.summary: Radiatively inefficient accretion flow grown from an equilibrium torus (Paczynski-Wiita potential, Shakura-Sunyaev alpha viscosity, gamma 5/3, r = 4-400 GM/c^2, log-spaced 256 x…
items.description: Radiatively inefficient accretion flow grown from an equilibrium torus (Paczynski-Wiita potential, Shakura-Sunyaev alpha viscosity, gamma 5/3, r = 4-400 GM/c^2, log-spaced 256 x 128 grid): the set-up of Duarte, Nemmen & Navarro (2022), regenerated with pinneapple_physics.blackhole. Density in the forecaster's window (r < 126.5 GM/c^2, theta in [pi/8, 7 pi/8]) every 20 GM/c^3 for t = 2000-10000 GM/c^3, whole trajectories per split. The training data of the black-hole weather forecaster (#399).

quality.label: source verified
quality.verification: Solver: mass and angular momentum conserved to 1e-16 with the boundary fluxes counted, exact Bondi accretion steady within 0.5 %, inviscid torus in equilibrium (tests/test_blackhole_weather.py). Resolution study (examples/black_hole_weather/convergence.py; results/convergence.json): grids 90x45, 128x64, 181x90, 256x128 (ratio sqrt 2), seeds 0-2 on every grid with the same seeded perturbation, time averages over t = 2000-10000 GM/c^3 with 95 % intervals (batch means and seeds). Converged within the statistical band (the two finest grids agree within their intervals): mean accretion rate 2.18 +- 0.58 (181) vs 1.97 +- 0.63 (256), window mass 2.65e4 vs 2.58e4, inner density slope -0.41 vs -0.38, persistence error at 100 GM/c^3 0.0034 +- 0.0011 vs 0.0047 +- 0.0011. Not converged: from 181 to 256 the time-mean profiles change more than between the coarser grids (density 6.3 % vs 0.8-1.6 %, specific angular momentum 4.2 % vs 0.5 %, angular-momentum flux 11 % vs 1.5-2.5 %; l / l_Kepler at r = 10 rises 3.8 % beyond its interval), so the observed order is negative and no GCI applies; the number of cells where the speed / temperature ceilings act grows with resolution and is the likely cause. The 256 x 128 grid is the finest the study could afford (a 362 x 181 run did not finish); the 181 -> 256 changes are the uncertainty band of these data. The published PLUTO runs and the paper's values could not be retrieved for a direct comparison.

items.description: Non-dimensional channel [0, 10] x [0, 1], Re 100, Pr 0.71: parabolic inlet with time-varying mean velocity U(t) in [0.6, 1.4] and inlet temperature 0, no-slip walls, adiabatic except a heater on the bottom wall at x in [2, 4] with flux -dT/dy = Q(t) in [0, 2], zero-gradient outlet. After a 15-unit warm-up each trajectory records u, v, p, T on the 128 x 32 cell centres every 0.4 time units over 40 units (101 snapshots), with the actuators and the quantities of interest (bulk outlet temperature, maximum temperature, pressure drop, heat in / out, stored energy). Training actuation is random holds, steps and ramps; two test splits use families never seen in training (chirped sinusoids, steps between the range edges), for digital-twin and forecasting models. Cell centres and all solver settings are in meta.json; fields[:, k] is the state at t = 0.4 k.

items.name: cylinder_wake_lbm
items.title: Confined cylinder wake, lattice-Boltzmann, Re 20-100 (9 runs, 720 vorticity snapshots, 240 x 100)
items.summary: 2-D flow past a cylinder (diameter D = 20 lattice cells) 3 D downstream of a uniform inlet in a channel 5 D high and 12 D long (blockage 0.2), no-slip walls, pressure outlet;…
items.description: 2-D flow past a cylinder (diameter D = 20 lattice cells) 3 D downstream of a uniform inlet in a channel 5 D high and 12 D long (blockage 0.2), no-slip walls, pressure outlet; D2Q9 BGK lattice-Boltzmann, inlet velocity 0.1 (Mach 0.17), no turbulence model. Each run covers 200 convective units (t U / D); the last 40 are stored (saturated wake), a vorticity snapshot (normalised by U/D, 0 inside the cylinder) every 0.5 units, labelled by Reynolds number, wake regime (steady or shedding), Strouhal number and wake amplitude. For regime classification, interpolation in Re and wake forecasting. The channel is far shorter than the entrance length, so the cylinder sees a nearly uniform inflow with thin wall boundary layers. Grid: x = i, y = j lattice cells, cylinder centre and solid cells in meta.json.

quality.label: source verified
quality.verification: Solver checks (python scripts/zoo/cylinder_data.py verify; pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.cylinder_wake.verify): developed low-Re channel flow against plane Poiseuille, max profile error 7.6 % / 4.3 % on the 2x coarser / dataset grid (first order, full-way bounce-back walls), centreline over mean velocity 1.43 / 1.46 vs 1.5. Resolution study at Re 100 (D = 20, 30, 40 lattice cells, same physical time and sampling): Strouhal 0.2444 / 0.2458 / 0.2460, so the dataset grid (D = 20) is within 0.7 % of D = 40; vorticity rms 2 D behind the cylinder within 0.3 %; transverse-velocity rms within 6.7 % (0.9 % at D = 30). At Re 120, D = 20 gives a Strouhal number 4.4 % below D = 30 (relaxation time 0.55, near the stability limit), so the dataset stops at Re 100. Every shedding run is saturated: the probe rms changes by at most 5 % across the stored window; below the onset (Re <= 50, confinement delays it from the unconfined ~47) disturbances decay. Strouhal number from a Hann-windowed, peak-refined spectrum (raw FFT bins are 0.025 apart). All fields finite.

items.summary: A neodymium-like cylinder magnet falls along the axis of a wire loop. The 3-D field of the magnet is computed at every instant (vector potential and Biot-Savart of its bound…
items.description: A neodymium-like cylinder magnet falls along the axis of a wire loop. The 3-D field of the magnet is computed at every instant (vector potential and Biot-Savart of its bound surface current), the flux through the loop by Stokes' theorem, and the EMF = -dPhi/dt. Checked against Maxwell's coaxial-circle formula, the free-fall time at which the EMF changes sign, and the net flux change over the whole fall; the field in time is the animation.

items.title: FDTD in 3-D + time: configurable sources and materials, mesh convergence (3D+t)
items.summary: A 3-D FDTD study configured by a plain dict (domain, cells per wavelength, sources, materials). The default runs a Hertzian dipole in vacuum on a refinement ladder: the radiated…
items.description: A 3-D FDTD study configured by a plain dict (domain, cells per wavelength, sources, materials). The default runs a Hertzian dipole in vacuum on a refinement ladder: the radiated power (near-to-far-field transform) against the closed form, with the observed order, the Richardson-extrapolated value and the GCI; the Maxwell residuals of the field in x, y, z and t (pp.maxwell); then the configured case (the dipole beside a dielectric sphere) on the same ladder: no closed form exists, so it reports its extrapolated value, observed order and GCI against a declared accuracy target. The 3-D field in time is the animation and an interactive three.js viewer.

items.name: examples/science/electromagnetism/research_inverse_permittivity
items.title: Inverse problem: permittivity of a slab from its reflection spectrum (1D)
items.summary: A dielectric slab of unknown permittivity and loss is measured in reflection: the 'measurement' is a 1-D FDTD run (with the CPML, the scheme's dispersion and added receiver…
items.description: A dielectric slab of unknown permittivity and loss is measured in reflection: the 'measurement' is a 1-D FDTD run (with the CPML, the scheme's dispersion and added receiver noise), the model is the transfer-matrix reflection of pp.em.waves.multilayer. Least squares recovers eps_r and the conductivity with their covariance. The model lacks the scheme's dispersion, which biases the fit by about one standard uncertainty: the instrument is simulated at the fitted point and the bias of that noiseless refit is removed, with its own uncertainty. The recovered values are compared with the truth the measurement was generated from (hidden from the fit), and the fit is repeated on noise realisations to check the stated uncertainty (coverage, centring).
